common_name: Black Aztec Corn (Black Mexican Sweet Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows once soil has warmed, since wind pollination in isolated single rows gives poor ear fill.

directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows once soil has warmed, since wind pollination in isolated single rows gives poor ear fill. Black Aztec dates to at least the 1860s in Mexico and the American Southwest and was long grown as a dual-purpose corn: pick the ears for fresh eating while the kernels are still pale cream and milky-sweet, or leave them on the stalk to dry, when the kernels darken dramatically to a glossy blue-black prized for cornmeal and corn flour. Its old-fashioned, richly sweet flavor at the milk stage made it a garden favorite before modern sugary hybrids replaced open-pollinated sweet corns, and the jet-black dried ears remain popular for autumn decoration as well as grinding.

common_name: Seneca White Corn (Haudenosaunee White Flour Corn)

planting.note: Sow in blocks of several short rows in fertile soil, hilling stalks slightly as they grow; let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvest and shelling.

directions: Sow in blocks of several short rows in fertile soil, hilling stalks slightly as they grow for stability, and let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvest and shelling. Seneca White is a traditional white flour/flint corn central to Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) agriculture in what is now upstate New York, grown for generations alongside beans and squash in the Three Sisters planting system. The soft, starchy white kernels are traditionally parched, ground, or simmered into corn soup, and community-led seed-saving efforts such as the Iroquois White Corn Project have kept this culturally vital variety in cultivation after it nearly disappeared from wider circulation in the twentieth century.

common_name: King Philip Corn (Historic New England Flint Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow once the soil has warmed, in blocks rather than single rows; its short season lets it succeed even in cool, short-summer regions.

directions: Direct sow once the soil has warmed, in blocks rather than single rows, and take advantage of its short season to succeed even in cool, short-summer regions of northern New England. King Philip is one of the oldest documented flint corns in cultivation, recorded in Massachusetts and Rhode Island since colonial times and traditionally said to honor the Wampanoag leader Metacomet, known to English colonists as King Philip. The eight-rowed ears bear hard, deep red-brown kernels that dry quickly on the stalk and grind into a flavorful, reddish cornmeal long used for johnnycake and other traditional New England cornbreads.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

common_name: Longfellow Flint Corn (New England Yellow Flint Corn)

planting.note: Plant in blocks after the soil has warmed; its short, reliable season suits northern New England gardens.

directions: Plant in blocks after the soil has warmed; its short, reliable season makes it well suited to northern New England gardens where longer-season dent corns struggle to dry down before frost. Longfellow is an old New England eight-row yellow flint corn, kept in circulation by regional seed savers and small farms in Maine and neighboring states for its dependable yields and cold-season resilience. Ears dry hard and quickly on the stalk, and the kernels grind into a sweet, full-flavored yellow cornmeal typical of the flint corns that sustained early New England farm households through winter.

common_name: Roy's Calais Flint Corn (Vermont Abenaki Flint Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as danger of frost passes; among the most cold-adapted flint corns available.

directions: Direct sow as soon as danger of frost passes; this is among the most cold-adapted flint corns available and reliably dries down even in short, cool Vermont-style growing seasons. Roy's Calais Flint traces to Abenaki agriculture in the Calais, Vermont area and was preserved through the twentieth century by farmer Roy Fair before seed steward Sylvia Davatz continued growing and distributing it, making it one of the best-documented survival stories among Northeastern landrace corns. Ears show a striking mix of yellow, red, and burgundy kernels on the same cob, and the corn is prized both for cornmeal and for polenta with a distinctively rich, sweet flint-corn flavor.
